text_to_speech: Welcome, my name is Dr. Scott Melideo, and in this short under 5-minute video, we are to take the tools that we have learned about in previous videos of this series and use them to write the name and formula for a binary ionic compound with a transition metal. 1st we will go from the name to the formula. We will start with the name iron(II) chloride. The main difference when working with a transition metal is that we have parentheses after the name of the transition metal that will tell us the charge. And you may be asking yourself why? And the reason is that transition metals can have multiple charges to them, and this is the way we let people know what that charge is on the metal. The (II) means that the iron has a +2 charge. As for the chloride since it’s a halogen it has a minus one charge. Based on that information please pause the video and try to write the chemical formula yourself. Did you get FeCl2? If not let’s using our crossover method. Do you see it now? If not, that is okay. Let’s try another example, nickel(III)oxide. Please pause the video to give yourself enough time. The answer to this is Ni2O3. Again, you can check your work by using the cross over method, as shown. Now let’s move on to going in the other direction with the following example FeO. The tip here is always look at the anion to help figure out the charge on the transition metal. The reason to do this is that you should know the charge on the anion. In this case the charge on oxide is minus 2. To determine the charge on our transition metal let’s use the formula that was mentioned in an earlier video if you didn’t watch that video this is the formula we are going to work with: the number of cation atoms times the charge of a cation plus the number of anion atoms times the charge of an anion equals zero. Using the given information, we can set up the equation to look like this: one iron atom times X since we don’t know the charge on the iron plus one oxygen times the charge of a single oxygen, -2 must equal 0. Solving for X, we have 1X plus -2 equals 0. Add 2 to both sides of the equation, and we get X equals a positive two. This means that the charge on our iron is a positive two. Then to write the name we would write it as iron(II)oxide don’t forget your roman numeral. Now it’s your turn to try with this next example, CuI2. Pause the video here to give yourself enough time to answer. Hopefully, you got copper(II) iodide. If not let’s use that formula again: 1 copper times X plus 2 iodides times -1 equals zero. We then get 1X plus -2 equal 0. Add 2 to both sides, and we get X equals positive 2 and remember the X is the charge on our copper. In the next video we will cover ionic compounds that contain a polyatomic ion. I hope this was helpful. Thank you for taking the time to watch this video!

youtube_description:
This video highlights the difference in naming Ionic compound when you have a transition metal present versus a metal from the main group elements.
This is the second to last video in a series of videos related to ionic compounds.
